blocks.content: IT Onboarding and Offboarding Policy
1. Purpose

This policy defines how the company provisions IT systems access for a new employee or contractor, and how it revokes that access when the person leaves or changes role. Consistent onboarding gets new hires productive on their first day without ad hoc requests to individual system owners, and consistent offboarding closes the most common source of unnecessary standing access: former employees and contractors whose accounts were simply never disabled.

This is also one of the controls most frequently sampled during a SOC 2 audit, since access-termination timeliness is a direct, easily-tested indicator of whether access control is actually being enforced day to day rather than only on paper.

Getting onboarding right matters as much as getting offboarding right: a new hire who spends their first week chasing down access requests forms an early impression of the company's operational maturity, and a hiring manager who cannot predict when their new report will actually be productive cannot plan the first sprint around them.

This policy is intentionally the single source of truth for the question 'who currently has access to what, and why' from an identity-lifecycle perspective. Individual system owners still decide the specific permissions within their own tool, but the trigger events — a person joining, changing role, or leaving — and the timeliness expectations around each are standardized here so that no system's access lifecycle depends on a system owner remembering to check the HR roster on their own initiative.
2. Scope

This policy applies to every employee, intern, and contractor who receives a company identity and any associated system access, regardless of location or employment type. It covers the standard baseline access every new hire receives (identity provider account, email, chat, laptop management enrollment) as well as the role-specific access requested separately by the hiring manager, and it covers both a full offboarding (departure) and a partial one (internal role change that should narrow access rather than only add to it).

Physical badge access to office locations is provisioned and revoked using the same trigger events described in this policy, but the underlying badge system itself is administered by Facilities and is documented separately.

Interns and fixed-term employees follow the identical onboarding workflow as any other employee, with one difference: their identity-system record carries an expected end date from day one, sourced from the offer terms rather than left open-ended, so that an intern whose term simply concludes without a separate departure action does not rely on someone remembering to manually trigger offboarding weeks after their actual last day.

Vendor personnel who are issued a company identity for the duration of an engagement — for example, an embedded contractor from a staffing partner, or a vendor engineer given temporary access to debug an integration — are also in scope, though their access is always time-boxed to the engagement's contracted end date rather than left open-ended the way an employee's access is by default.

A leave of absence — parental leave, medical leave, or an extended sabbatical — is handled as a third category distinct from either onboarding or offboarding: access is suspended rather than fully revoked, and the identity system records an expected return date so that IT Support can proactively restore access ahead of the person's return rather than waiting for a ticket on their first day back. An unplanned extension of leave triggers a re-confirmation of the expected return date rather than an indefinite suspension.
3. Roles & Responsibilities

Onboarding and offboarding both depend on a timely, accurate signal from HR — a start date, a role, a manager, and, on departure, a last day of work. Everything IT Support does downstream depends on that signal arriving on time.

Security Engineering's role is deliberately upstream of individual requests rather than in the approval path for every one: it defines the tiering rules that IT Support and hiring managers apply day to day, so that routine onboarding does not bottleneck on a security review for every single new hire, while still ensuring that the rules those day-to-day approvals rely on are sound and current.

Two terms recur throughout §4 and are worth defining precisely here: baseline access is the identity provider account, corporate email, chat, and device management enrollment every employee receives regardless of role; role-specific access is any additional system or data access requested separately and tied to the specific responsibilities of the person's job. This distinction determines both who can request an access grant and how quickly it must be revoked when no longer justified — baseline access is removed automatically on any departure, while role-specific access is what the periodic review in §4.4 exists to keep honest over time.

blocks.content: 4. Procedure

Onboarding and offboarding are mirror images of the same workflow, both driven by an HR system event and both routed through IT Support for execution. Role-specific access beyond the baseline is provisioned according to the tiering and approval rules of the Access Control and Least Privilege Policy (POL-006), §4.

blocks.content: 4.1 Onboarding

HR creates the new-hire record at least five business days before the start date wherever possible, which gives IT Support time to provision baseline access and ship a laptop ahead of day one. The hiring manager submits role-specific access requests separately, referencing the least-privilege tiering rules in POL-006, §4, so that a new hire's day-one access matches their role rather than defaulting to whatever the previous person in the role happened to accumulate over time.

Baseline access — identity provider account, corporate email, chat, and device management enrollment — is provisioned automatically from the HR record without a separate manual request, since every employee needs it regardless of role.
4.2 Role Changes

An internal transfer or role change is treated as a partial offboarding followed by a partial onboarding: the new manager requests access appropriate to the new role, and the previous manager confirms which access tied to the old role should be removed. Access is not carried forward by default on the theory that it might still be useful; it must be re-justified for the new role.

This is the scenario IT Support sees go wrong most often in practice, because unlike a departure it has no hard deadline forcing the old access to be revoked: an employee who moves from Support into Engineering, for example, tends to keep their old support-tooling access long after they stop needing it, simply because removing it was never anyone's single clear responsibility. The quarterly access review in §4.4 exists partly to catch exactly this pattern.
4.3 Offboarding

HR creates the departure record as soon as a departure date is known, ideally in advance for a planned departure and immediately for an involuntary one. IT Support disables all system access — identity provider, email, chat, VPN, and every role-specific system granted under POL-006 — no later than the end of the employee's last working day, and immediately in the case of an involuntary termination flagged as high-risk by HR or Security.

Disabling an account is distinct from deleting it: accounts are disabled immediately and retained for a standard 90-day window before deletion, so that a manager can request read-only access to a departed employee's mailbox or files during an ownership handoff without needing to restore anything.
4.4 Verification and Access Reviews

IT Support reconciles the HR system's active-employee list against every system's active-account list on a monthly cadence, specifically to catch any offboarding step that was missed. Any account found active for a person no longer with the company is disabled the same day it is found, and the gap is logged for the quarterly access review.
4.5 Contractor and Time-Boxed Access

A contractor's access is provisioned with an expiration date matching the engagement's contracted end date whenever the identity system supports it, rather than relying on someone remembering to disable the account manually when the contract ends. If the engagement is extended, the hiring manager must submit an explicit renewal before the original expiration date; access does not lapse gracefully into an indefinite grant simply because no one got around to disabling it.

IT Support reviews all time-boxed accounts nearing expiration on the same monthly cadence used for the general reconciliation in §4.4, flagging any that are approaching expiry without a renewal on file so the hiring manager has advance notice rather than a surprise access cutoff mid-engagement.
4.6 Involuntary and High-Risk Terminations

HR and Security jointly flag a termination as high-risk when the circumstances suggest an elevated chance of retaliatory or unauthorized action — for example, a termination for cause, or a departure during an active performance or security investigation. A high-risk termination triggers immediate access disablement timed to coincide with the termination conversation itself, rather than at end of day, and Security additionally reviews that person's recent access logs and any data export activity in the preceding 30 days as a standard part of the offboarding checklist.

Coordinating the exact timing of a high-risk termination is a joint responsibility of HR, the Engineering Manager, and IT Support, communicated through a dedicated, restricted channel rather than the standard offboarding ticket queue, precisely because premature or delayed access disablement in this scenario carries meaningfully higher risk than in a routine, amicable departure.
4.7 Rehire Handling

A former employee or contractor who rejoins the company is provisioned as a new hire under §4.1 rather than having their old, disabled account reactivated, even if that account still exists within the 90-day retention window described in §4.3. Reusing an old account risks silently restoring access tied to a role the person no longer holds, and it complicates audit trails that assume one identity maps to one continuous employment record.

If a rehire's prior account is still within its retention window, IT Support completes deletion of that account as part of processing the rehire, rather than leaving two accounts for the same person to coexist. HR's system of record links the two employment records so that tenure-based benefits and access history remain traceable across the gap, even though the underlying IT accounts are entirely separate.
4.8 Shared and Service Accounts

This policy governs individual human identities; shared accounts and non-human service accounts are provisioned and reviewed under the Access Control and Least Privilege Policy (POL-006), §4, not under this policy, even though the initial request may originate from the same onboarding conversation. A common failure mode this distinction is meant to prevent is a departing employee's individual credentials being quietly repurposed as a de facto shared account for a task their team still needs done — any such need is instead provisioned as a proper service account through POL-006 rather than surviving as leftover access under a disabled human identity.

When a new hire's role involves administering a shared or service account — for example, rotating a service account's credentials as part of the quarterly cycle described in the Access Control and Least Privilege Policy — that responsibility is granted through the standard role-specific access request in §4.1, and is removed the same way any other role-specific access is removed on departure or role change.
4.9 Remote and International Onboarding

A new hire joining from outside the country where the company's primary IT infrastructure is based follows the same baseline and role-specific provisioning workflow, but laptop shipping and any hardware-token-based access (used for the most sensitive Critical-tier systems under POL-006) are initiated further in advance — HR is expected to create the new-hire record at least ten business days ahead of the start date for an international hire, rather than the standard five, to account for customs and shipping variability.

Where local employment law restricts what access can be granted before a formal employment contract is countersigned, IT Support provisions a limited pre-start account sufficient for orientation and paperwork but withholds production-system access until the Engineering Manager confirms the contract is fully executed, so that the standard start-date SLA in Table 2 is measured from contract execution rather than from the originally targeted start date in that specific case.
4.10 Escalation When the HR Signal Is Late or Missing

IT Support's ability to meet every SLA in Table 2 depends entirely on receiving a timely, accurate HR event; when a start date changes, a manager reassignment happens after access has already been requested, or a departure record is created later than the actual last working day, the standard workflow alone cannot recover the missed timing after the fact. IT Support escalates any HR record discovered to be late, missing, or inconsistent with a manager's direct report to the HR/People Team lead the same business day it is discovered, rather than silently absorbing the delay into its own SLA measurement.

A pattern of late or missing HR records — three or more in a rolling quarter — is raised by IT Support to the Security Engineer as an audit-relevant finding in its own right, independent of any single instance, since a systemic delay in the HR signal is exactly the kind of root cause that produces the 'former employee whose account was never disabled' scenario this policy exists to prevent, regardless of how promptly IT Support itself acts once a record does arrive.
4.11 Equipment Return and Asset Tracking

Every laptop, mobile device, and hardware access token issued at onboarding is recorded against the employee's identity in the asset management system, and its return is tracked as a distinct checklist item from access disablement rather than assumed to happen automatically alongside it. IT Support confirms equipment return within five business days of a planned departure's last working day, and immediately opens a lost-asset investigation with Security if equipment is not returned and not accounted for by an approved exception, such as an employee purchasing their own device at departure under a documented program.

A device that is not returned and cannot be confirmed wiped is treated as a potential data exposure and escalated to Security the same way a lost or stolen device would be at any other point in an employee's tenure, since an unreturned laptop that still holds locally cached credentials or documents is a real risk regardless of whether the underlying account access has already been disabled.
4.12 Manager and Approver Changes Mid-Process

It is not uncommon for a new hire's manager to change between offer acceptance and start date, or for an approver of a pending role-specific access request to leave the company or change roles before acting on it. IT Support treats a pending access request whose approver is no longer in that role as blocked, not silently approved or silently dropped, and re-routes it to the new manager or the approver's own manager for a fresh decision rather than assuming the original intent still holds.

A new hire whose assigned manager changes before their start date has their onboarding record updated by HR as soon as the change is known, and any role-specific access requests already submitted by the outgoing manager are reviewed and re-confirmed by the incoming manager before provisioning proceeds, so accountability for what access a new hire receives always traces back to whoever is actually accountable for their work on day one.
5. References

Access Control and Least Privilege Policy (POL-006), §4 — the tiering and approval rules used when provisioning role-specific access during onboarding, and the access this policy revokes on offboarding.

External standards: SOC 2 (AICPA Trust Services Criteria) (https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2), which routinely samples offboarding timeliness as a logical access control; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (https://www.iso.org/standard/27001), Annex A.5 human resource security controls.

Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4 — governs onboarding and offboarding of vendor personnel supplied by a staffing partner or integration vendor, distinct from the company's own employee HR record but following an analogous access lifecycle.

The HR system's new-hire and departure event feeds, and the identity system's provisioning automation referenced throughout this policy, are maintained jointly by HR Systems and IT Support; this document defines the accountable roles and SLAs, not the technical configuration of that automation.
